summary: The lecture covers salient features of the Indian Constitution, including its written nature, sources from various constitutions, blend of rigidity and flexibility, federal structure with unitary features, parliamentary system, independent judiciary, fundamental rights, directive principles, fundamental duties, secularism, universal franchise, single citizenship, emergency provisions, three-tier government, independent bodies, cooperative societies, and major criticisms.
points: Original Constitution had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules.
Written Constitution ensures constitutional supremacy; unwritten (UK) ensures parliamentary supremacy.

Borrowed features: US (Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review), UK (Parliamentary System, Single Citizenship), Canada (Strong Centre, Residuary Powers), Ireland (DPSP), Japan (Procedure Established by Law), Russia (Fundamental Duties), Germany (Emergency Suspension).
Blend of rigidity and flexibility: Art. 368 requires special majority; some amendments by simple majority (Art. 3, 4); Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
Federal with unitary features: Art. 1 "Union of States"; quasi-federal (K.C. Wheare); bargaining federalism (Morris Jones); cooperative federalism (Granville Austin).
Parliamentary government at Centre and States: nominal head (President/Governor), real head (PM/CM), collective responsibility, executive part of legislature.
Independent integrated judiciary: Supreme Court apex; appoints/transfers High Court judges; Court of record.
Fundamental Rights (Part III, Art. 12-35) qualified; enforced via Art. 32 (SC) and Art. 226 (HC); Art. 19 suspended only during external aggression; Art. 20, 21 non-suspendable.
DPSP (Part IV) non-justiciable; three categories: Socialist, Gandhian, Liberal-Intellectual; balance with FRs evolved judicially.
Fundamental Duties added by 42nd Amendment (1976) on Swaran Singh Committee; 11 duties under Art. 51A; 86th Amendment added duty to educate children 6-14.
